lessons.title: Two minutes in the box
lessons.objective: Name the common minor penalties and what happens after one.

payload.prompt: Match the foul to a two-minute minor penalty.

pairs.definition: Using the stick to hold or impede an opponent; a two-minute minor.
Bringing someone down with stick or leg; a two-minute minor.
Stick contact above the shoulders; a minor or double minor if blood.

explanation.summary: These are the most common minor penalties you'll hear called all night long.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hooking, tripping, high stick: these three you'll see constantly.

payload.prompt: What happens when a player is called for a two-minute minor?

options.text: They sit in the penalty box; the other team gets a man advantage (power play)
They are ejected from the game
The team pays a fine and keeps playing 5-on-5

explanation.correct: Exactly. A minor sends the player to the sin bin for two minutes. Meanwhile, the other team plays 5-on-4 (or however many skaters vs the shorthanded team has). The penalty ends early if a goal is scored.
explanation.incorrect: A two-minute minor means the player sits in the penalty box while the opposing team has a power play (one extra skater). It's the most common penalty in hockey.

payload.prompt: Match the penalty to what causes it.

pairs.definition: Using the stick to hold or impede an opponent; two-minute minor.
Bringing an opponent down with the stick or a leg; two-minute minor.
The stick makes contact above the shoulders; can be a minor or double minor if it draws blood.

explanation.summary: These are the stick fouls that call minors. They are the bread and butter of referee calls; you'll hear them all night.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hooking and tripping: those are the calls you see all the time.

payload.prompt: A two-minute minor penalty ends as soon as the power-play team scores. True or false?

scene.alt: A player sits in the penalty box while the opposing team scores on the power play, and the shorthanded player is waved out.

explanation.correct: True. When the power-play team scores, the penalty ends immediately and the player comes out of the box. This is why a goal cuts short a power play.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a goal on the power play ends the minor penalty. The player comes out of the box and regular play resumes at full strength.

payload.question: What just happened?

options.text: Number 7 used their stick to hold an opponent
Number 7 is going to the penalty box for two minutes
The other team gets a power play
Number 7 will be ejected if they do it again

payload.translation: The referee called hooking on number 7, meaning they used their stick to hold or impede an opponent. They go to the box for two minutes while the other team gets a man advantage.

followUps.line: How long was that power play?
followUps.why: Tests if you understand it ends early with a goal.

followUps.line: Could the high stick also be a minor?
followUps.why: Shows you know different infractions have different penalties.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Refs call hooking and tripping constantly; you'll get used to them quickly.

lessons.title: Stick fouls: high stick, holding, interference
lessons.objective: Distinguish the stick and contact minors.

payload.prompt: Match the stick foul to its description.

pairs.definition: The stick makes contact above the shoulders; a minor, or a double minor if it draws blood.
Using the arms or body to impede an opponent without the puck; a two-minute minor.
Checking or impeding an opponent who does not have the puck; a minor that protects the puck carrier.

explanation.summary: These fouls interrupt play and result in time in the box. The distinction matters: holding and interference are body fouls, high stick is the stick.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's holding; you can't do that to a player without the puck.

payload.prompt: A high stick that draws blood is a four-minute double minor. True or false?

scene.alt: A player's stick makes contact with an opponent's face and blood is visible.

explanation.correct: True. A high stick that draws blood is a double minor (four minutes total). If a goal is scored during the first two minutes, the second minor still applies.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, when a high stick draws blood, it's automatically a double minor: four minutes, two consecutive minors. The first minor can end early with a goal, but the second begins.

payload.prompt: Which of these is holding?

options.text: Using your arms to pin an opponent against the boards
Checking a player who has the puck
Touching the stick of an opponent who has the puck

explanation.correct: Right. Holding is using your body to impede an opponent who doesn't have the puck. Checking is legal; holding is not.
explanation.incorrect: Holding is when you use your arms, body or stick to prevent an opponent from moving, especially one without the puck. It's a two-minute minor.

payload.prompt: Complete the double minor rule.
payload.template: A double minor is {{duration}} of penalties. If the power-play team scores during the first {{minutes}}, the second minor {{happens}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A double minor is four minutes: two consecutive minors. A goal on the power play ends the first minor but starts the second.
explanation.incorrect: A double minor means four minutes of penalties served as two consecutive two-minute minors. A goal during the first two minutes ends the first but begins the second.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That's holding. You can't grab a player without the puck like that.

payload.question: What did the player do?

options.text: They used their body to prevent someone from moving
The player they grabbed did not have the puck
It will be a two-minute penalty
It was a legal check

payload.translation: Holding means using your body or arms to stop an opponent without the puck. It's not a legal check; it's a two-minute minor.

followUps.why: Tests if you know they're similar but distinct fouls.

followUps.line: What if the stick was involved?
followUps.why: Shows you know the difference between stick fouls and body fouls.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Holding and interference are cousins; refs call them when you grab someone without the puck.

lessons.title: Boarding, charging, cross-checking
lessons.objective: Recognize the dangerous fouls that draw majors.

payload.prompt: A major penalty is five minutes in the box. True or false?

scene.alt: A player sits in the penalty box with an angry expression; the scoreboard shows a five-minute penalty timer.

explanation.correct: True. A major is five minutes, served in full, even if the power-play team scores. Majors are for dangerous fouls like fighting, boarding or cross-checking.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a major penalty is five minutes. Unlike a minor, a goal does not end a major; it runs its full duration. Majors often come with suspensions.

payload.prompt: What is boarding?

options.text: Driving an opponent into the boards with force; can be a minor or major depending on how hard
Checking an opponent who is standing on the boards
Using the boards to push yourself away from an opponent

explanation.correct: Exactly. Boarding is a dangerous hit into the boards. A minor boarding is a two-minute penalty; a dangerous boarding can be five minutes or more, and may draw a suspension from the Department of Player Safety.
explanation.incorrect: Boarding means aggressively hitting an opponent into the boards. It's a penalty for a dangerous hit. The severity depends on the impact.

payload.prompt: Match the dangerous foul to its description.

pairs.definition: Driving an opponent forcefully into the boards; a minor or major depending on severity.
Taking more than two strides before checking an opponent; building up speed for a hard hit.
Using the shaft of the stick (not the blade) to check an opponent; dangerous because of the leverage.

explanation.summary: These are the dangerous fouls that often draw majors or suspensions. They exist to protect player safety.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's a cross-check; the stick shaft across the body, that's five minutes.

payload.prompt: Complete the major penalty rule.
payload.template: A major penalty is {{duration}} minutes and {{goal-rule}}.

explanation.correct: Right. A major is five minutes, always served in full. A goal does not end it.
explanation.incorrect: A major penalty lasts five minutes regardless of scoring. It's served in full because it's for a dangerous foul.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That was boarding on the replay. He drove him into the boards pretty hard; five minutes and probably in the Department of Player Safety's office tomorrow.

payload.question: What is the ref saying?

options.text: The player made a dangerous hit into the boards
It could be reviewed for a suspension
It's a five-minute major penalty
The player will be ejected from the game

payload.translation: Boarding is aggressively driving an opponent into the boards. A five-minute major is on the ice; a suspension comes later if the league reviews it.

followUps.line: Will he be back for the next game?
followUps.why: Tests if you know majors and suspensions are separate.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Majors and suspensions are different; a major is on the ice, a suspension comes from the league.

lessons.title: Misconducts, ejections and fights
lessons.objective: Explain game and match penalties and what a fighting major is.

payload.prompt: Complete the misconduct penalty rule.
payload.template: A game misconduct sends a player out for the rest of the game and lasts {{duration}}. The team goes {{strength}} because it's just an ejection, not a penalty.

explanation.correct: Right. A game misconduct is a ten-minute ejection with no power play; the team stays at full strength. It's about removal, not punishment on the scoreboard.
explanation.incorrect: A game misconduct means the player is gone from the game (ejection). The ten minutes is mainly for the record; the team does not go shorthanded.

payload.prompt: What happens if two players start fighting?

options.text: Each gets a five-minute major penalty; the team goes down one skater each during the five minutes
Both players are ejected and the team goes shorthanded
Each gets a misconduct and both teams are at full strength

explanation.correct: Exactly. Fighting majors are five minutes each. Both teams sit a player, making it 5-on-4... wait, no, both are down, so it's still 5-on-5. The majors run in parallel.
explanation.incorrect: A fighting major is five minutes for each player involved. Since both teams lose a player, it stays 5-on-5 the whole time. The fight is rare these days in the NHL.

payload.prompt: Match the ejection type to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A ten-minute ejection ending the player's game; no power play, team stays at full strength.
An ejection for intent to injure; the rarest penalty in hockey, given for truly dangerous behavior.
A five-minute major for each player in a fight; both teams go down one, so it stays 5-on-5.

explanation.summary: These are the serious consequences: ejection, long-term penalties, and the possibility of suspension. Fighting is allowed in the NHL but rare; the PWHL and international hockey treat it as a punishable infraction.
explanation.sayThisLine: Game misconduct, he's done for the night.

payload.prompt: Fighting majors make the game 4-on-4 because both teams lose a player. True or false?

scene.alt: Two players are escorted to opposite penalty boxes after fighting.

explanation.correct: False. Both teams lose one player, so it stays 5-on-5 the whole time. The two penalties run in parallel, not sequentially.
explanation.incorrect: It stays 5-on-5 because both teams are down a player. One fight, two majors, parallel time, same strength. This is why fighting majors don't create power plays.

payload.question: What just happened?

options.text: Number 18 is ejected from the game
The team does not go shorthanded
It's a ten-minute penalty (for the record)
A goal will end this penalty

payload.translation: A game misconduct is an ejection. The player leaves, but the team stays at full strength (no power play given up). It ends only at the end of the game or when the ten minutes expire.

followUps.line: Is he done for the season or just tonight?
followUps.why: Tests if you know a misconduct is just an ejection, separate from suspension.

followUps.line: What's the difference between a misconduct and a fighting major?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A misconduct means ejection; the Department of Player Safety decides about suspension later.

lessons.title: The power play, in one sentence
lessons.objective: Explain what a man advantage is and how it ends.

payload.prompt: What is a power play in one sentence?

options.text: One team has a man advantage because the other is serving a penalty
A team scores a goal while playing fast
Two teams play 5-on-5 after a stoppage

explanation.correct: Exactly. A power play is when you have more skaters than the other team because they have a player in the box. A 5-on-4 is the most common.
explanation.incorrect: A power play is a man-advantage situation: your team has more skaters on the ice because the other team is serving a penalty. It ends when the penalty time expires, a goal is scored, or you get another penalty.

payload.prompt: A power play ends when one of three things happens.
payload.template: A power play ends when {{first}}, {{second}}, or {{third}}.

explanation.correct: Right. You score (early end), the penalty time expires (full time), or the foe gets a penalty (becomes 4-on-4).
explanation.incorrect: A power play ends when: (1) you score, (2) penalty time expires, or (3) the shorthanded team gets a penalty.

payload.prompt: A 5-on-4 power play happens most often because of what?

options.text: A two-minute minor penalty on the other team
A five-minute major penalty on the other team
The opponent pulled their goalie

explanation.correct: Correct. A two-minute minor gives you 5-on-4 power play. A five-minute major also does, but those are rarer. A 5-on-3 is the biggest advantage (two minors at once).
explanation.incorrect: A 5-on-4 is the most common power-play scenario, resulting from a two-minute minor. A major also creates a power play, but minors are more frequent.

statement.speaker: Announcer
statement.text: And that's a power-play goal! One-one!

payload.question: What does that mean?

options.text: The team scored while on the power play
The score is now tied at one goal each
The other team's penalty is now over
The game just went to overtime

payload.translation: A power-play goal means the team with the man advantage scored. The penalty ends immediately (for minors) and play resumes at even strength.

followUps.line: Does a power-play goal count differently than a regular goal?
followUps.why: Tests if you know it's worth the same (1 point) but with context.
Shows you know PP% is goals ÷ power plays.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Power-play goals are huge momentum shifts; fans love them because they show special-teams execution.

lessons.title: Surviving a penalty kill
lessons.objective: Describe what the shorthanded team is trying to do.

payload.prompt: When a shorthanded team scores while on the penalty kill, what is it called?

options.text: A shorthanded goal
An even-strength goal
A defensive goal

explanation.correct: Right. A shorthanded goal (or 'shorty') is when the team down a man scores. Fans love them because they flip the momentum instantly and end the penalty.
explanation.incorrect: A shorthanded goal happens when the penalized team scores while defending. It's rare, exciting, and instantly ends the penalty.

payload.prompt: Match the penalty-kill strategy to what it does.

pairs.definition: Four players form a tight box to protect the slot and force perimeter shots; a passive strategy.
The shorthanded team pressures the puck carrier to force turnovers; a risky but potentially rewarding strategy.
Get the puck out of your zone and run out the clock; the most basic goal of the penalty kill.

explanation.summary: A penalty kill is a defensive job: protect the slot, clear the puck, and run out the penalty time. A goal is a bonus.
explanation.sayThisLine: They run a box on the penalty kill: solid, predictable.

payload.prompt: A successful penalty kill means the shorthanded team did not allow a goal. True or false?

scene.alt: The clock shows the penalty time expired and the scoreboard has not changed.

explanation.correct: True. A kill means you got through the penalty without giving up a goal. You don't need to score (though a shorty is incredible); you just need to survive.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a penalty kill means the penalized team survived without allowing the power-play team to score. A shorty is better than that.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: Our penalty kill is 82 percent. Top five in the league. That's winning defense.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: The team kills 82 out of every 100 penalties
This is a key stat for the team's success
The penalty kill is a defensive unit that prevents power-play goals
The team has not allowed a goal in the last 82 minutes

payload.translation: Penalty kill percentage (PK%) is the share of penalties killed without allowing a goal. 82% means 82 out of every 100 power plays are stopped. A strong penalty kill is crucial.

followUps.line: What's a good penalty kill percentage?
followUps.why: Tests if you know ~80% is average.

followUps.line: How does this compare to the power play?
followUps.why: Shows you understand PK% and PP% are related stats.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Penalty kill is a specific job; players who are good at it are often specialists on the fourth line.

payload.prompt: Order these manpower situations from most to least advantageous for the team on the power play.

items.why: The biggest advantage: five skaters against three; about 90 seconds of 5-on-3 is common.
The most common power play: one extra skater for two minutes.
Actually no power play at all; even strength with fewer skaters, very wide open.

explanation.correct: Right. 5-on-3 is the best advantage, then 5-on-4, then 4-on-4 (no power play).
explanation.incorrect: A 5-on-3 is the most lethal. A 5-on-4 is standard. A 4-on-4 is no power play; just even strength with fewer skaters.

payload.prompt: When does a 5-on-3 happen?

options.text: Two players on the same team are in the penalty box at the same time (two minors)
One team has a minor and the other gets a major
A power-play team scores without ending the penalty

explanation.correct: Exactly. A 5-on-3 is when one team has two penalties running at once. This is usually caused by a sloppy play: two infractions in quick succession. It's the most dangerous power-play setup.
explanation.incorrect: A 5-on-3 power play means the shorthanded team has two players in the box. This is rare and lethal; teams often score from a 5-on-3 because the two-man advantage is huge.

payload.prompt: Complete the 4-on-4 rule.
payload.template: When both teams get minors at the same time, the result is {{result}}, not a power play. This creates {{effect}} hockey because there are {{total}} skaters instead of {{normal}}, so the ice is wide open.

explanation.correct: Right. A 4-on-4 (mutual minors) is wide-open hockey: four skaters per side instead of six, so both teams have tons of ice. It's exciting but unpredictable.
explanation.incorrect: When both teams get a minor, the penalties cancel out into a 4-on-4: no power play for either side. Eight total skaters (four per side) instead of ten makes the game look like a wide-open track meet.

payload.prompt: A 5-on-3 power play is about 90 seconds in duration because one of the two minors expires while the other continues. True or false?

scene.alt: The scoreboard shows two penalty timers, one expiring before the other.

explanation.correct: True. A 5-on-3 usually lasts about 90 seconds (one player comes out), then it becomes a 5-on-4 for the rest. This is why 5-on-3 is so scary: only 90 seconds of the best advantage.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a typical 5-on-3 is 90 seconds because the two minors don't expire at the same time. After 90 seconds, one player returns and it becomes a standard 5-on-4.

lessons.title: Penalty shots and embellishment
lessons.objective: Recognize a penalty shot and a dive.

payload.prompt: When is a penalty shot awarded?

options.text: When a player is fouled from behind on a clear breakaway, preventing a goal-scoring chance
When a team gets five penalties in one period
When a player shoots and misses the net

explanation.correct: Right. A penalty shot is one-on-one against the goalie: the fouled player skates from the center line and tries to score with no defenders. It's a huge gift because most breakaways would not score anyway.
explanation.incorrect: A penalty shot is awarded for a foul on a breakaway. The player gets a one-on-one chance at the goalie, starting from center ice with a running start. It's one of hockey's most exciting moments.

payload.prompt: Match the scoring opportunity to its description.

pairs.definition: A one-on-one against the goalie awarded for a foul on a breakaway; starts from center ice.
A team advantage because the opponent has a player in the box; multiple attackers against full defense.
A best-of-three one-on-one competition to break a tie after 3-on-3 overtime (not used in NHL playoffs).

explanation.summary: A penalty shot is the rarest and most dramatic way to score. It's not a power play; it's a single chance, one shot, one goalie.
explanation.sayThisLine: Penalty shot! He was fouled on the breakaway.

payload.prompt: Embellishment is when a player exaggerates or fakes a foul to draw a penalty. True or false?

scene.alt: A player falls dramatically after minimal contact from an opponent.

explanation.correct: True. Embellishment (or 'diving') is when a player sells a foul that didn't happen, exaggerates, or falls theatrically. Refs can call embellishment on the diver if they spot it.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, embellishment is faking or exaggerating a foul. It's a minor penalty against the diver. Fans hate it because it's dishonest, and refs punish it inconsistently.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That was a dive. He barely got touched and threw himself on the ice. Two minutes for embellishment.

payload.question: What did the player do?

options.text: They exaggerated or faked a foul
They got caught embellishing and drew a penalty against themselves
The contact was minimal but they sold it theatrically
They were rightfully awarded a penalty shot

payload.translation: Embellishment is selling a foul that didn't happen. If the ref catches the diver, they call embellishment on that player (two minutes). Fans dislike diving.

followUps.line: Does he get a penalty shot if he's caught diving?
followUps.why: Tests if you know embellishment is a penalty against the diver, not a reward.

followUps.line: How often do refs call embellishment?
followUps.why: Shows you know it's called inconsistently.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Diving is one of the most debated things in hockey; fans and refs disagree on when it's called.
